item.title: If that's where community is, that's where I want to be.
item.description:
Honestly, I'm not that familiar with Discord. To me, it seems like one of the million ways to chat with people that already exist, like Teams and messages and email and blah, blah, blah. The fact that it's kind of gamer focused is useful. But ultimately, I'm trusting my gut and what my students have to say about it being a good place to collaborate and evolve this game, and hopefully build a community.

That's what I'm really going after here. If that's where community is right now, that's where I want to be.

Setting it up

Setting it up was super easy with help from Claude. The server has a handful of channels: #general for hanging out, #playtest-notes for bugs and "this is too hard," #art-and-ideas, and three channels the game fills in by itself: #changelog, #devlog and #stats.

The game posts its own updates

Here's the trick. Discord lets you make a webhook for a channel: a private link where anything sent to it shows up as a post. The game's code lives on GitHub, and GitHub can run little jobs on a schedule or whenever something changes. So now:

  • Every evening, GitHub rounds up that day's builds and posts them to #changelog.
  • When a memo goes live, like this one, it lands in #devlog with its cover.
  • Every morning, after the play-stats summary, the numbers go to #stats.
  • When new art comes in, it goes up in #art-and-ideas.

The webhook links are kept as GitHub secrets, so they never sit in the public code. And GitHub remembers what it already posted, so nothing shows up twice.

The first time I saw the game post its own changelog and stats without me touching anything, I was thrilled. One less thing for me to worry about while I'm working on making the game better.

Out in the open

The stats are the part I like most. Every morning you can see how many people played, how far they got, and what killed them. Group Chats are winning right now.

I love the idea of transparency, and of this being a potential learning tool for others who want to try to build a game. And community at the same time.

What I hope you find there

Say someone finds the server six months from now. I want them to find a thriving community, and a way to check what's been done in the game and how we got there. I think that will be important for other people who want to try the same thing, or something similar, or even people trying to learn how to code, like myself. This has direct implications for what I'm doing in EMAT, and it's a really cool way to explore all that code can do.

Next for the server: your screenshots, your bug reports, maybe a weekly challenge. All of the above.

And while you're here: two new stages are coming after the minimap, the hospital and the home neighborhood. Vote for which one comes first in the quick poll on the devlog's sidebar.

Join the Midlife Survivors Discord. Come say hi, tell me what's too hard, and watch the game update itself.

What changed

  • A Midlife Survivors Discord server, open to everyone
  • The game posts its own changelog every evening
  • New memos land in #devlog automatically
  • Morning play stats in #stats, out in the open
  • New art goes up in #art-and-ideas when it lands

Next up: A minimap that fills in as you explore, then two new stages you can pick: the hospital and the home neighborhood. And Abdel's music.

item.title: This is starting to feel real.
item.description:
V2 means this is starting to feel real. Somewhere between the 3 a.m. feedings, Election Day, doctor's appointments and keeping the house tidy, this thing I've been thinking about for months is actually taking shape, and it feels good.

If the kid version of me, building websites on GeoCities, could see what I built today, he wouldn't believe it. I remember what the internet was like when people's passions were websites, blogs and communities. I want to go back to that.

This started out as a way to deal with being off work. I'm not very good at taking time off, and I've been told over and over not to work on work while I'm on paternity leave. So I'm putting my energy into something I want to see go out into the world. Kinda like the twins.

Then and now

V. 1.47 next to today. Pick a screen and drag the slider.

The title screen

I love the new title screen. It ties the game to the website and makes them feel like a single unit. I love all the key art, but these are my favorites, because it's starting to feel more personal. Like a part of me is coming to life in the game.

Four of them had been retired from the title screen because the menus covered the characters. I brought them back, so the slideshow has nine scenes now.

Clocking in

Runs feel good. The lights react to your weapons now, the office is full of people, and TJ and Derek show up mid-run. But I'm worried it might still be too hard for new players. That's where I need help from playtesters and feedback. Join the Discord! The next post will go into this a little more.

The exit interview

When you die now, HR sits you down for an exit interview, and whatever got you stands there looking smug about it.

And at 63.5 the Gold Watch shows up. You can't kill it. Every hit just winds the clock back a little, and all you can do is buy time until you clock out at 65. The idea came from the Grim Reaper in Vampire Survivors. Just a little less dark. Kinda.

GOTCHA!

The interns don't just walk up anymore. TJ and Derek show up with a coffee, a burrito or a bundt cake, and you have to chase them down. Catch one and the game slows for a beat, a GOTCHA! card stamps in with their portrait, and a little reel spins to land on your treat: a heal, a shield and a bonus. The coworkers at their desks got real bodies too, with chairs, legs and their own little habits.

Clock in anywhere

Your employee file can follow you now. Sign in with Google once, and your coins, unlocks, achievements and even a run in progress move between your phone, tablet and laptop. It's optional. Your file still saves on your device either way, and there are new Privacy and Terms pages in plain words.

Twice the gear

There are 13 new things to pick up: seven weapons and six passives. Mom's Spaghetti heals you while you stand in it, noise-cancelling headphones block hits, a rolling office chair bowls through crowds, Reply-All chains from enemy to enemy, Out-of-Office slows everything near you, sticky notes trap whatever steps on them, and Thermostat Wars freezes the room. But you only get six weapon slots and six passive slots, so you have to pick a play style: Healing, Shield, Offense or Defense. Chests only upgrade what you already carry now, and if a level-up only offers something new, you can skip it and heal a little instead.

Retirement is a party

Make it to 65 and the Gold Watch stops. A clock-out station appears with balloons and presents. Walk up, punch out, and you're retired. It used to be a reaper. Now it's a party.

The office filled in

The walls aren't bare anymore. Every room has shelves, clocks, posters and its own clutter, and the coworkers at their desks sit, stand and fidget. Bosses that charge into a wall bounce off it now (BONK) and need a second to shake it off.

A few fixes too. If your graphics drop out, the game saves your run and offers a reload instead of going white. Group Chats only shoot at you from where you can see them. The office uses about a third less graphics memory, and the title screen scrolls properly on short laptop windows.

While I was writing this

The game kept going. Full Life (40 to 100) got its own bosses: the HOA President charges with a yardstick, the Retirement Audit stamps out rings of forms, and the 6 AM Pickleball Champ lunges in loops. At 100, Father Time waits to shake your hand. Sticky Notes actually stick now. And there's a new Sprint mode, like Hyper in Vampire Survivors: beat the Midlife Crisis V8 to unlock it, and the years fly by twice as fast for 25% more 401(k).

Next time: the game got a Discord

I still don't totally get Discord, but my students say it's the place to be. So the game has its own server now, and it posts its own updates: a changelog every evening, new memos when they go up, and play stats every morning. The next memo is about how that works. Come say hi.

Who helped

Derek, TJ and Ben have really been into this project. Their playthroughs and thoughtful feedback helped earn them spots in the game. My oldest son, Abdel, is working on music for the game, too. This isn't just an AI project. It's becoming a truly collaborative experience.

The AI crew did their parts: ChatGPT drew the art, Gemini wrote a lot of the lines, Grok ran the balance numbers, Fable reviewed the whole build, and Claude put it together with me.

A special shout-out to my newborn twins, my beautiful wife and my super talented son. They're the real inspiration behind this project.

What changed

  • The Gold Watch: an unbeatable final boss you can only wind back until 65
  • Spotlight cards for heroes, bosses, rooms, interns and big moments
  • Dynamic lighting: weapons, enemies and bosses light up the dark
  • A new HR Exit Interview with defeated heroes and smug killers
  • Five new title scenes with the whole cast, drawn for phones too
  • The Coldwar Cowboy, TJ and Derek, and a rack with a yellow note
  • Faster on phones: lighter loading, smoother late game, instant Quick Retry
  • GOTCHA!: chase down TJ and Derek for a heal, a shield and a treat
  • Clock in with Google: your employee file follows you to any device
  • Twice the gear: 13 new weapons and passives, 6 weapon and 6 passive slots, four play styles
  • Retirement at 65 is a party: walk up to the clock-out station and punch out
  • Coworkers with real bodies, dressed-up walls, and bosses that bounce off walls
  • Safer runs: auto-save if your graphics drop out, plus lighter memory use
  • Full Life bosses: the HOA President, the Retirement Audit, the Pickleball Champ, and Father Time at 100
  • Sprint mode: years pass 2x faster for +25% coins, unlocked by beating the V8
  • Balance, writing and art passes from Fable, Grok, Gemini and ChatGPT

Next up: Next memo: the game got its own Discord, and it posts its own updates. After that: Abdel's music, a redone Lounge, and bosses for the Full Life years.

item.title: My friends work here now.
item.description:
My friends work here now.

TJ and Derek are two of our student photographers at UCM. They jumped in early, played the game way more than they had to, and sent me bugs and ideas before I'd even finished my coffee. Today they became interns at the office. Ben, a friend since 2002, became a whole new hero.

It felt good to put my friends in the game, especially the ones who showed up first. Their feedback has a direct effect on how this thing is coming together, and now you can see them in it.

TJ found the force field

TJ texted me this morning: on his second run in the same browser, enemies stopped chasing him and seemed to bounce off "like a forcefield around my character." A hard refresh fixed it. He was right, and he'd basically found the cause himself.

The enemies follow a map that rebuilds a few times a second around wherever you are. It kept time with the run's clock. When you start a new run, that clock goes back to zero, but the map still remembered the old time. It thought it had just updated, so it froze around the spot where your last run ended, and the enemies followed arrows pointing somewhere you weren't.

// A new run restarts the run clock at 0. Without this, the map froze around
// the spot where you died and enemies steered away from you.
if (now < lastBuild) { lastBuild = -1e9; lastPc = -1; ready = false; }

One line. TJ also asked for a way to test the late game without playing 15 minutes to get there, so now there's a dev console with god mode, any upgrade and a jump to any age. Scores never post while it's on. (Add ?dev=1 to the game's address once, then tap the DEV MODE chip. ?dev=0 turns it off.)

Coffee, snacks and a Lounge

TJ's other note was that runs end too fast because there aren't many ways to heal. So I asked Grok to work out the numbers, and now:

  • Birthdays heal you. At 45, 50, 55, 60 and 65 the break room springs for cake.
  • Elites drop a Desk Salad. It heals more than pizza, but it wilts in 14 seconds, so you have to go get it.
  • The interns bring you things. Every minute or so, TJ or Derek walks over with a snack, a coffee or a boost. If a Bill bumps into them, they run.
  • The Lounge opens after every promotion. One of them works the Break Room counter for about 35 seconds. Walk up, the game pauses, and you shop with your 401(k).

TJ and Derek came up with the Lounge in our group chat while I was asking them for lines. TJ sent me his. "What were the dinosaurs like?" and "For my Manager!!!" are both in the game now, and adding them made me smile.

The Coldwar Cowboy

Ben and I met in 2002, when I started at Kent as an undergrad. We both worked IT for the journalism school. So he's in the game as an IT guy with a soft spot for days gone by.

He throws a floppy disk that comes back to him. And once a run, when things get bad, he does the thing every IT person has said a thousand times: "Have you tried turning it off and on again?" The screen clears and he gets back up. You unlock him by reading 10 of these memos, which means you're about to be one memo closer.

One experience

The part I'm proudest of today is how it all feels together. The game, this devlog and the About page share one look now: the same fonts, the same memo strips, the same progress bar. Your stats follow you from the title screen to the devlog. The title tells you what version you're playing and what's new.

On a phone, it went from a wall of buttons to a poster you scroll.

And there are Spotlight cards. When a boss walks in, a coworker opens a new room, or you play a hero for the first time, a big card slides in with their sprite and one line, written by Gemini. That's the closest anything has come to the game I saw in my head before I started.

I want this to feel polished. Not a website for a game, or a game with a website, but one experience that makes the whole thing better.

How it gets made

I'm using Claude to coordinate everyone, AI and people. Grok does the math, Gemini writes the jokes, ChatGPT draws and builds rooms, and Muse tells me how my posts will land. My friends play it and tell me what's broken. Claude reads all of it and puts it together.

Also new today: the office got proper lighting, life after 50 now comes with surprises like "Rent Hike" and "Reading Glasses" for a couple of years at a time, and if you make it to 65 the office throws you a retirement party.

What changed

  • Fixed the second-run force field TJ found
  • Birthday cake, the Desk Salad and interns who bring you coffee
  • The Lounge: a counter shop in the Break Room after every promotion
  • New hero: the Coldwar Cowboy (read 10 memos)
  • Spotlight cards for bosses, rooms and new hires
  • Lighting, age 50+ surprises and a retirement party

Next up: Derek's own intern lines, Ben's jokes, and more playtesting with the crew.

item.title: I got promoted four times before lunch.
item.description:
How this image was made: Made with Grok (image generation), from a prompt Claude wrote and Rami directed: 16-bit pixel art in the game's palette, the 9-to-5er raising his coffee under a PROMOTED banner as a garage door rolls up and golden light pours out. Read the full prompt.

Last night my game was two rooms and a locked door. Today you can get promoted four times before lunch.

That's the big one. Every five years you get promoted, a door rolls up like a garage, and the office gets bigger. You start in the Lobby and the Bullpen. At 45 the Parking Lot and Break Room open. At 50, the Server Room and three glass Conference Rooms. At 55, the Executive Wing. At 60, the Wellness Corner, which HR built so you'd stop asking about raises. item.title: My office got jokes. Then my enemies got smarter.
item.description:
A week ago my office was a hallway. A long, beige, very professional hallway, with a couple of desks and the same three plants on a loop. It looked like a place where nothing has ever happened.

Now there's a car parked in the break room with a wheel boot on it. The sign says it's Dave's idea.

The office got jokes

I sent ChatGPT my list of things that are funny about office life (KPIs, "let's put that in the parking lot," motivational posters that have given up) and asked for them to become actual objects. Corporate slang, taken literally.

There's a traffic roundabout in the hallway that says CIRCLE BACK. A gauge on the wall stuck on MEH. A kiddie pool with a diving board for deep dives. A pot on a hot plate that is, yes, boiling a tiny ocean. And a framed sign that says KPIs, with a sticky note underneath: "What the hell is a KPI again?" (The full joke pops up at the bottom of the screen the first time you walk past each one. Once per run, so you aren't reading the same memo every lap.)

Then the enemies got smarter

All that furniture created a problem I didn't see coming. My enemies only knew one move: walk straight at you. Put a desk in the way and they'd walk into it and just... stay there. Like a Roomba that has accepted its fate.

I could stand behind a cubicle and the entire swarm would politely wait on the other side. That's not a game. That's a waiting room.

The fix is something called a flow field, and it's one of my favorite things I've learned so far. Instead of every enemy figuring out its own route, the game figures it out once, from where you are standing, and writes "steps to reach you" on every square of the floor. Each enemy just walks toward a smaller number.

// Flood outward from the player, one step at a time.
// Every open floor cell gets a number: how many steps to reach you.
while (n > 0) {
  const i = pop(), d = dist[i];
  for (const [dx, dy, cost] of NEIGHBORS) {
    const j = neighborOf(i, dx, dy);
    if (blocked[j]) continue;          // desks, cars, the kiddie pool
    if (d + cost < dist[j]) { dist[j] = d + cost; push(j, d + cost); }
  }
}

One flood, a few times a second, and three hundred enemies all know how to get around the desk. In my test, a group of donuts behind a desk reached me zero times with the old code. With the flow field, they were on me in two seconds. (It also means enemies can't spawn inside furniture anymore, which was happening. Bills were being born inside filing cabinets. Honestly, relatable.)

Close Calls

Once the enemies were smart, I wanted dodging them to feel good. Grok designed a whole system for it (seriously, its spec was 500 lines), and I built it: when something heading right at you misses by a hair, you get a Close Call. A little XP, a quick burst of speed, and a streak meter that climbs from CLOSE CALL to SIDE-STEP to OUT OF OFFICE to PERFORMANCE EXCEEDED.

The popups are my favorite part: "Not today, autopay." "Left it on read." "HR saw nothing."

And there was a lesson in building it. The design measured "close" using the player's size, 32 pixels. But the box the game actually uses to decide if you got hit is bigger, 48 by 52. So every "near miss" was secretly a hit. The test caught it on the first try. What you see isn't always what collides.

Real people played it

This is the part that got me. People actually played this week and told me what was wrong.

Ben said the game moves so fast he couldn't read the messages at the bottom of the screen. He was right. Now the important stuff (a boss showing up, the Comfort Zone Tax, power-ups) flashes in big letters right above your character.

T.J. said Dad Joke was useless, because you basically had to let enemies hug you for it to work. Also right. Now everything inside the groan circle stops to cringe and staggers backward. It buys you room instead of costing you health. Which, as any dad will tell you, is what a good joke is supposed to do.

I also started counting (anonymously) how long runs last and how far people get, so I can balance with real numbers instead of my own thumbs. So far, more than a dozen people have put their names on the leaderboard, and plenty more have played without one. (No names, no tracking cookies. Just run length, age reached and what got you. There's a note on the About page if you want the details.)

Next up

ChatGPT is building the first piece of the new office: a real Lobby and Bullpen, with doors that unlock as you get older, like promotions. The Executive Wing opens at 55. Of course it does.

If you played this week, thank you. If you haven't, go see if you can make it to OUT OF OFFICE. And come tell me about it in the Discord.

What changed

  • Office props: corporate slang taken literally, with jokes on approach
  • Enemies walk around furniture (flow field)
  • Close Calls: rewards and a streak meter for near misses
  • Playtest fixes: center flash banners, a stronger Dad Joke
  • Anonymous play stats

Next up: The new Lobby and Bullpen, with doors that unlock as you age.

item.title: There's a coffee button now. It feels weird.
item.description:
There's a new button on the main menu. It's cream colored, it sits right next to Devlog, and it says BUY THE DEV A COFFEE.

I went back and forth on that button for a while, because asking for money feels weird. I've been a photographer for twenty-some years. I know how to send an invoice for work somebody hired me to do. Putting out a tip jar for a game nobody asked for uses a totally different muscle, and mine is out of shape.

So I want to be upfront about where the money goes.

The coffee is mostly AI

This game is being built by one photographer and a handful of AI tools. Claude writes most of the code. ChatGPT draws the art. Gemini and Grok review the design and push back on it. I bring the vision, the jokes and the "no, that doesn't feel right yet."

Those tools aren't free, and they aren't unlimited. Right now I'm at my weekly limit with Claude. I burned through a whole month of Gemini in one day. (Some of that is my own fault. Every session ends with updated docs, a progress log, a textbook chapter and a devlog post. That paperwork eats usage. It's also the whole point: I want people to see how this thing actually gets made, mistakes included.)

So any early tips go to more AI time to get this game finished. Higher plans, more sessions, more art passes. If there's ever more than that, I'll tell you here first. (It goes through Ko-fi, which keeps 0% of one-time tips. PayPal or Stripe still take a small processing cut.)

Why now

Four days ago, my wife and I had twins.

I'm not going to pretend that doesn't matter. Two new humans is real financial pressure, and like everybody, I wish I made a little more. But that's not what this button is for. Holding a newborn at 3 a.m. just made it clear to me that I want to finish the things I start, and to let my kids see me make things I care about. (In this house the 3 AM Thought is basically a documentary now.)

So I'm throwing my net out. Not for a payday. For people.

Looking for my crew

What I'd really love is to find a small group of people who want to see this game get made, and maybe help make it.

  • Play it and tell me what's wrong. Too easy, too hard, not funny, funny in the wrong place. Playtest notes are gold.
  • Bring a skill. Pixel art, sound, music, game design, code, writing jokes about the DMV. If any of that is you, I'd love to talk.
  • Share it with a friend who just turned 40. They'll get it.
  • Buy a coffee if you want to and can. It keeps the AI running.
  • Join the Discord. That's where playtests, art previews and the crew live.

The button itself is about the smallest piece of code in the whole game:

// Ko-fi tip jar: opens in a new tab so your run stays put
bindNavItem(coffeeBtn, 10, () => {
  window.open("https://ko-fi.com/ramidaud", "_blank", "noopener");
});

That "_blank" means it opens in a new tab. I asked for that on purpose. If you're nice enough to buy me a coffee, the least I can do is not lose your game.

No coffee required

Everybody's budget is spoken for, mine included. Playing, sharing, or telling me the Donut is too strong helps this project just as much. If you want to get involved, come say hi in the Midlife Survivors Discord. There's a #want-to-help channel waiting for you.

Now go survive a few years. I'll be over here, running on very little sleep and whatever AI time I have left this week.

What changed

  • Buy the Dev a Coffee on the main menu and Game Over screen
  • Ko-fi links in the devlog header, footer and About page
  • Early tips go to AI usage to finish the game

Next up: Reviewing the first batch of real enemy art from ChatGPT.

item.description:
Here's an embarrassing thing to admit about your own game: four minutes in, I could put the controller down.

My weapons were doing so much damage that I could stand in one spot and let midlife come to me. Bills, robocalls, donuts, all of it melting before it got close. Nineteen minutes felt like the right length for a run. The run itself just wasn't a fight.

That's backwards. In Vampire Survivors you die a lot early on, buy a few upgrades, and come back a little stronger. A first-time player should not get anywhere near the end.

So Claude hired a robot

I didn't know how to measure "too easy," so Claude built a little bot that plays the game. (It's not a smart bot. A real person lasts about three to four times longer than it does, so its numbers are a floor, not a forecast.) It dodges enemies, walks toward gems and picks perks at random. Then it ran three bots at the same time on a fast-forwarded clock: a brand-new player, a half-upgraded one and a fully upgraded one.

The numbers were rough. A fully upgraded bot standing completely still lasted 13 minutes. One run banked over 5 million coins, which buys the entire shop in one go. My weapons were killing enemies faster than the game could spawn them.

The fix: the game grows with you

Now enemies get tougher and more numerous every time you level up. Bosses scale with your level and your age. Hits hurt more after 48. Coins come in slowly, so the 401(k) Shop is something you work toward over a lot of runs.

Leveling up keeps you even. Permanent upgrades are how you get ahead. Here's what that looks like in the actual file. Every one of these numbers is a dial I can turn:

hpPerLevel: 0.10,     // enemies get 10% tougher for every level YOU gain
packPerLevel: 0.35,   // ...and show up in bigger groups
bossHpPerYear: 0.10,  // bosses get 10% tougher for every year past 40
hitDamageByAge: [[40, 0], [48, 1], [55, 2], [62, 3]], // hits hurt more at 48, 55 and 62

Then I got a second opinion

I asked Grok to review the difficulty too. (Grok's notes came back as a document I handed straight to Claude. Two AIs passing notes through me, like a group project where I'm the only one who shows up to meetings.) It came back with a full handoff document: bugs (one perk claimed to boost "all weapons" and quietly skipped three of them), tuning numbers, and some new ideas. Claude worked through it in order.

Two of those ideas made it in. Tax Bracket is an optional difficulty you can crank from "Standard Deduction" up to "Full Audit" for bigger rewards. And my favorite, the Comfort Zone Tax: go 45 seconds without getting hit and the game sends extra enemies for 20 seconds.

dynamic: {
  armAfterMs: 90000,        // off for the first 90 seconds of a run
  noHitBonusAfterMs: 45000, // go 45 s without getting hit...
  bonusPackAdd: 2,          // ...and every group gets 2 extra enemies
  bonusDurationMs: 20000,   // for 20 seconds. That's the Comfort Zone Tax.
}

I played it at 1 AM with newborn twins asleep down the hall. It feels a lot more like Vampire Survivors now. I died. I wanted to go again.

What changed

  • Enemies and bosses scale with your level
  • Coins come in slowly; the 401(k) Shop is the long game
  • Tax Bracket: optional difficulty with bigger rewards
  • Comfort Zone Tax: 45 seconds without a hit brings more enemies

Next up: Near-miss rewards for dodging, then the art pass.

item.title: The office has seen a few restructurings.
item.description:
The characters can walk now, so I wanted the office around them to feel more like a place.

The first environment pass is Accounts Payable. It has the three desk personalities, a printer with a paper jam, an overstuffed filing cabinet and a plant that could use a day off. (It's no coincidence that PTO Day is also a pickup in the game. It clears the whole screen. The plant would like one too.) The floors have carpet and wood patterns now, with warmer lighting and a few scattered signs of office life.

One thing I'm learning: background detail has to stay quieter than the action. (Photographers know this one. If the background is as busy as the subject, nobody knows where to look. Same rule in a game, except the subject is being chased by donuts.) The floor can have texture without competing with the person trying to survive on it. The furniture also needs to block the right amount of floor space so walking around it feels believable.

Even the jokes live in a data file. Each department gets a landmark and a line you see when you walk in:

{ id: 'accounts', name: 'ACCOUNTS PAYABLE',
  landmark: 'The paperwork skyline',
  joke: 'Every pile has been marked urgent since 2009.',
  // three desk personalities, placed on the 32-pixel grid
  desks: [[-928, -544, 'tidy'], [-768, -544, 'paperwork'], [-608, -544, 'lunch']] }

This is still the separate art test. Next is deciding how much detail feels right before extending the look to the other departments and environments.

What changed

  • Three desk personalities in the Campus art test
  • Carpet and wood floor patterns, warmer lighting
  • Printer jam, filing cabinet, breakroom plant props

Next up: Decide how much detail survives before the other departments get the same look.

item.title: The office has people in it now. And they walk.
item.description:
The office layout felt good, but I wanted the graphics to feel more animated. So the next art pass was walking sheets (A sprite sheet is one image holding every frame of an animation in a grid. The game shows one square at a time, fast, like a flip book.) for all three playable characters: the 9-to-5er, the Soccer Dad and the Grad Student at 45.

They each have four directions and four walking poses per direction. You can switch between them in the separate art test and walk around the same desks. There's also a side-by-side preview so I can compare their movement before replacing the main game's art.

One useful detail: the walking animation follows distance traveled. (Most games loop the walk on a timer, so a character pushing into a wall moonwalks in place. Counting steps by distance fixes that.) If you push into a desk and stop moving, your feet stop too. Small thing, but it helps the character feel connected to the room. This is the whole trick:

// Each frame, add up how far the character actually moved.
walked += distanceWalked;

// Pick the walking pose from distance, not time: a new step every 17 pixels.
// Pushing into a desk means no distance, so the feet stop too.
currentFrame = CharacterArt.frame(facing, moving ? Math.floor(walked / 17) : 1);

These are the first walking sheets. The costumes and rhythm still need a look, then we can add idle and combat reactions.

What changed

  • Four-direction walking sheets for all three playable characters
  • Explore As switcher and direction gallery in the art test
  • Step timing tied to distance traveled

Next up: Judge the costumes and rhythm, then idle and combat poses.

item.title: I've never made a game. Here's a green dollar sign chasing a square.
item.description:
I'm a photographer. I've spent twenty-some years figuring out where to stand and when to press the button. I have never made a video game. Not a little one in college, not a Flash thing in 2006. Nothing.

But I've played a lot of Vampire Survivors. If you haven't: you walk around, your weapons fire on their own, and an absurd number of monsters try to touch you. That's it. It's the most relaxing stressful thing I own. (Vampire Survivors came out in 2022 from a tiny studio called poncle, and it started life as a browser game. That's part of why mine runs in a browser too.)

Somewhere around my forties I realized midlife works the same way. You don't get to choose your attacks anymore. You just keep moving while the bills, the robocalls and the weird new back pain close in.

So that's the game. Midlife Survivors. You start at 40. You survive.

The vision part (that's my job)

Before any code, I wrote down my Top 10 midlife annoyances. Bills. Phone calls. Diabetes. Fat. Work drama. Sleep. Aches and pains. Kids' math homework. Errands. Death.

That list turned into the enemies. A Bill chases you, and if you don't pay it off fast it splits into Late Fees. "Spam Likely" rings before it charges. Donuts slow you down if you touch them. Death shows up at the end and can't be beaten, because, well. (He got a promotion since this was written. In the main game, the ending at 65 is your Retirement Party. Death still waits at 100 in Full Life mode.)

The AI part (that's Claude's job)

I'm building this with Claude as my co-developer. I describe what I want to see and feel, and it writes the code and explains what it did in plain English. It's like working with a patient engineer who never gets tired of "wait, what's a game loop?" (A game loop is the bit of code that runs about 60 times a second: move everything, check what's touching, redraw the screen. Every single thing in the game happens inside it.)

The first thing we built was a square. You could move it with the arrow keys or by dragging on your phone. That's the whole game at that point: a square on an endless carpet.

Here's the code that moved it, from the very first build. The lines in green are Claude explaining itself, which is how I learned to read code at all.

// Read the keys: left/right and up/down each add or subtract 1.
let x = 0, y = 0;
if (cursors.left.isDown || keys.A.isDown) x -= 1;
if (cursors.right.isDown || keys.D.isDown) x += 1;
if (cursors.up.isDown || keys.W.isDown) y -= 1;
if (cursors.down.isDown || keys.S.isDown) y += 1;

// Normalize so moving diagonally isn't faster than moving straight.
const len = Math.hypot(x, y);
if (len > 0) { x /= len; y /= len; }

player.setVelocity(x * moveSpd, y * moveSpd);

That "normalize" bit was my first real lesson: without it, holding up and right at the same time makes you about 40% faster. Every game has to fix that.

Then a green dollar sign showed up and started chasing it. I laughed way harder than I should have.

The learning part (that's the point)

Every session ends with one new idea I actually understand. One of the first: the numbers don't live in the code. They live in small data files I can edit myself.

window.PLAYER = {
  startingAge: 40,
  speed: 220,        // pixels per second. Try 120 (tired) or 400 (too much coffee)
  maxHp: 10,         // your health. Each Bill touch costs 1
  hurtCooldownMs: 700, // after a hit, you're safe for this long
};

Another: a game redraws the screen about 60 times a second, and everything you see happens inside that loop. Move the player, move the enemies, check if they're touching, draw it all again. Sixty times. Every second.

That one blew my mind a little.

Next up: a coffee splash that fires on its own, and the first time I got hit by a Bill and died.

What changed

  • First playable square with touch and keyboard movement
  • First Bill (green $) chase
  • Top 10 midlife annoyances became the enemy roster

Next up: Coffee Splash that fires on its own, and the first real Game Over.
